hints.title: Negate the outer requirement first
hints.body: The definition requires every member a of the set to have a successful shared prime factor. Failure needs one member a for which that requirement fails.
hints.recap: Not every means there exists a failing member.
hints.pitfall: The exceptional a must remain a member of T.
hints.pause: Discard options still requiring the failure for every a.

recall.reminder: Negate one level at a time and preserve the domain.

hints.title: Negate the inner existence claim
hints.body: For the exceptional member, the definition asks for at least one prime witness with a specified property. Negating existence must rule out every successful witness.
hints.recap: One unsuccessful prime does not rule out a different successful prime.
hints.pitfall: Keep the prime’s entire required property together while negating.
hints.pause: Rewrite the inner requirement as a failed existence statement.

recall.reminder: One unsuccessful prime does not rule out a different successful prime.

hints.title: Preserve the scope of other
hints.body: A successful prime in the original definition only has to divide one other member. Check that your negation refers to precisely that success condition and preserves the membership restrictions.
hints.recap: Quantifier scope matters at every level.
hints.pitfall: Ruling out a prime shared by every other member is a different claim.
hints.pause: Assemble the outer and inner negations and match the full statement.

recall.reminder: Quantifier scope matters at every level.

solution:
T is not stapled exactly when there exists a member a of T such that there is no prime factor of a which divides at least one other member of T.

The outer every becomes there exists; the inner there exists a successful prime becomes there is no successful prime. The phrase at least one other remains part of what that prime would have to accomplish. Answer F.
